solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Typical of daughter to have a pop (4)

blocks.note: 'that's so him' means that's typical of him

annotation.surface: A remark that a daughter will naturally have a dad.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Pop' reads as father, beside 'daughter'; it is the fizzy drink. The 'a' does double service in the surface but gives its own letter here.
annotation.definitionFit: Soda is a pop, a fizzy soft drink.

entries.clue: In rows, pleb upset Flipper’s producer (4,6)

indicatorNotes.upset: the letters are knocked over into a new order

annotation.surface: A commoner annoyed by rows, and a nod to the TV dolphin Flipper.
annotation.walkthrough: Flipper is the famous TV dolphin, but in cricket a flipper is a leg-spin delivery that skids on low, so the man who bowls it is a spin bowler.
annotation.definitionFit: A spin bowler is the cricketer who delivers a flipper.

entries.clue: Love note is rubbish? Don’t start that! (5)

indicatorNotes.Don’t start: tells you to drop the first letter of 'that' word, SUCKS

blocks.note: 'sucks' means is rubbish; without its start it is UCKS

annotation.surface: Someone scolding a person for calling a love song rubbish.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Love' is not affection but a form of address: in northern England and the Midlands 'ducks' is a friendly way to say 'love' or 'dear'. 'That' points back at the slang 'sucks'.
annotation.definitionFit: 'Ducks' and 'love' are interchangeable British terms of endearment.

entries.clue: For example, a trinket or a treat (4,1,5)

blocks.note: a trinket is one example of a charm, the kind on a bracelet
as in 'it worked a treat', British for very well

annotation.surface: A list of little presents: a trinket or a treat.
annotation.walkthrough: 'A treat' reads as a noun, a present; it is the British phrase 'works a treat', meaning very well.
annotation.definitionFit: Both phrases describe something going perfectly: it worked a treat, it worked like a charm.

entries.clue: With paranoid leader out, checks for bugs (7)

indicatorNotes.out: a letter that is out is no longer in the word, so P goes

blocks.note: INSPECTS means checks; P is removed from it

annotation.surface: A paranoid boss gone, someone sweeps the office for listening devices.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bugs' in a paranoid setting suggests hidden microphones; here it means creepy-crawlies.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in everyday speech, though strictly bugs are one order of insects.

entries.clue: Nurse and sick medic confined to quarters? (7)

indicatorNotes.sick: the letters of MEDIC are unwell, so disordered

annotation.surface: A nurse and an ill doctor stuck in their rooms, as if in quarantine.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Confined to quarters' sounds like a soldier's punishment; the question mark lets it mean confined to certain regions, which is what an endemic disease is.
annotation.definitionFit: Something endemic is restricted to a particular area.

entries.clue: Carriages picking up duke and two queens? (5)

indicatorNotes.picking up: the carriages take the duke aboard, so D goes inside

annotation.surface: Royal coaches collecting a duke and a pair of queens.
annotation.walkthrough: The royal procession sets you looking for monarchs; the question mark flags that these queens are playing cards.
annotation.definitionFit: Two queens from a pack are two cards, an example of the answer.

entries.clue: Vehicle from which porters unload green cases? (9)

annotation.definition: Vehicle from which porters unload green cases?

blocks.note: reads as a luggage van at a station; the porters are hospital porters
reads as green suitcases or crates of greens; the cases are patients looking sick

annotation.surface: A lorry of luggage or produce crates being unloaded by porters.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Porters' and 'cases' suggest a station or market with suitcases or crates of green vegetables; in a hospital the cases are patients, looking green around the gills.
annotation.definitionFit: An ambulance delivers sick patients for hospital porters to take inside.

entries.clue: Premier being probed by head of Interpol (4)

indicatorNotes.being probed by: the letter pokes into the word, so it goes inside

annotation.surface: A prime minister under investigation by the international police.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Premier' reads as a prime minister, a noun; it is the adjective meaning chief.
annotation.definitionFit: Premier and main both mean foremost, as in the main event.

entries.clue: One prepping for one’s future retirement? (8)

annotation.definition: One prepping for one’s future retirement?

blocks.note: someone getting something ready in advance
reads as a pension; it is retiring for the night later on

annotation.surface: Someone planning for a pension.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Retirement' pulls towards pensions; it means retiring for the night. At Cambridge a bedmaker is also a college servant who tidies students' rooms.
annotation.definitionFit: A bedmaker gets a bed ready for someone to retire into later.

entries.clue: Awful acne is red as rose (9)

indicatorNotes.Awful: the letters are in a terrible state, so rearranged

annotation.surface: Bad acne as red as a rose.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Rose' looks like the flower of a simile; it is the past tense of rise.
annotation.definitionFit: Rose and increased both mean went up.

entries.clue: Novice with no time for teacher (5)

indicatorNotes.with no: the novice is left with no T, so that letter drops out

blocks.note: RABBIT, British slang for a poor player; T is removed from its end

annotation.surface: A beginner too busy to see a tutor.
annotation.walkthrough: In British sporting slang a 'rabbit' is a weak player, especially a hopeless batsman at cricket.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: rabbi is Hebrew for 'my master', the title of a Jewish teacher of the law.

entries.clue: Bargain outlets at front, a few finally going bust (5)

indicatorNotes.at front: take the front letters of 'Bargain outlets'
indicatorNotes.finally going: the last letter of SOME goes

blocks.note: first letters of Bargain and Outlets
'a few' is SOME, losing its last letter

annotation.surface: Discount shops with a few going bankrupt.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Going bust' reads as going bankrupt, which suits the shops; 'going' belongs to the wordplay and 'bust' stands alone as the chest.
annotation.definitionFit: Bust and bosom both mean a woman's chest.

entries.clue: Cold bud in Bordeaux only in undies (8)

annotation.surface: Someone in Bordeaux in the cold, wearing only underwear.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bud' tempts you towards a flower; it is a buddy, and 'in Bordeaux' asks for the French word.
annotation.definitionFit: A camisole is a loose sleeveless undergarment, one item of undies.
annotation.definitionNote: 'undies' is plural; a camisole is one piece of underwear

entries.clue: Pearls only put out for me in particular (10)

indicatorNotes.put out: the letters are disturbed into a new order

annotation.surface: Someone who wants only pearls set out for them.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition is a phrase used as an adverb: 'personally, I'd rather not' means speaking for me in particular.
annotation.definitionFit: Personally means as far as I am concerned, for me in particular.

entries.clue: Journo in broadcast about crackpots (7)

indicatorNotes.about: the word for broadcast turns round

blocks.note: to sow is to broadcast seed; reversed it is WOS

annotation.surface: A reporter on air talking about lunatics.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Broadcast' reads as TV or radio; it is the farming sense, scattering seed.
annotation.definitionFit: Whackos and crackpots are both slang for eccentric or crazy people.

entries.clue: A bit of advice in hearing for commissioner? (9)

indicatorNotes.in hearing: what you hear, not what you read

blocks.note: a pointer is a tip, a bit of advice

annotation.surface: A tip given at a hearing before an official.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Hearing' and 'commissioner' suggest an inquiry; 'in hearing' signals the sound-alike, and 'commissioner' means one who commissions.
annotation.definitionFit: A commissioner is one who commissions or appoints, an appointer.

entries.clue: Lilt and port consumed in some volume with drug (7)

indicatorNotes.consumed in: the port is swallowed inside the volume

blocks.note: cubic centimetres, a measure of volume

annotation.surface: Lilt, a British fruit soda, and port drunk with drugs.
annotation.walkthrough: Lilt is also a British soft drink, which sits with 'port' and 'consumed'; here it is the rise and fall of a voice.
annotation.definitionFit: A lilt is a rhythmic rise and fall, a cadence.

entries.clue: Fight that a couple of campanologists might start (4-4)

annotation.definition2: that a couple of campanologists might start

blocks.note: British slang for a noisy row

blocks.clueFragment: that a couple of campanologists might start
blocks.note: the sound two bells make in turn

annotation.surface: Two bell-ringers squaring up for a fight.
annotation.walkthrough: Campanologists are bell-ringers; the second half reads as them starting a brawl, but it is the sound of two bells.
annotation.definitionFit: In British slang a ding-dong is a heated argument or fight.

entries.clue: Ran out of old wine private eye opened (7)

indicatorNotes.opened: the wine is opened up and the detective put in

annotation.surface: A detective opening a bottle of old wine and then running out of it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Ran out of' reads as a phrase; 'of' only joins, and 'Ran out' is the definition, as a passport runs out.
annotation.definitionFit: Something that ran out, like a licence, has expired.

entries.clue: Orders and awards good to go for conservative (7)

indicatorNotes.to go for: G leaves and C takes its place

annotation.surface: Honours and prizes switching from a good cause to a Tory one.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Orders' and 'awards' together look like honours such as the Order of the Garter; 'Orders' is the definition, meaning commands.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a decree is an order issued with official authority.

entries.clue: Hard test head brought back for impish kids (7)

indicatorNotes.head brought back: the first letter moves to the end

blocks.note: a stinker is a very hard exam or task; its head S goes to the back

annotation.surface: A tough exam paper handed back to naughty pupils.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Brought back' tempts a full reversal; only the head moves. In British speech a 'tinker' is a mischievous child.
annotation.definitionFit: Little tinkers are mischievous, impish children.

entries.clue: Note-taking Parisian very attached to crime (7)

indicatorNotes.taking: the French word takes the note inside
indicatorNotes.attached to: ON is joined on at the end

annotation.surface: A Parisian jotting notes, deeply involved in a crime.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Attached to' does two jobs: it gives ON and says where it goes.
annotation.definitionFit: Treason is the crime of betraying one's country.

entries.clue: One once in Split broadcast I covered (8)

annotation.surface: A reporter who once lived in the Croatian city of Split describing their coverage.
annotation.walkthrough: The capital S dresses 'Split' as the Croatian port; it is a split between partners, and a divorcee is one who was once in it.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by description: the marriage split up, so this person was once in it.

entries.clue: Alternative dam has no piece of masonry (5)

indicatorNotes.has no: the dam 'has no' M, so that letter is dropped

blocks.note: a dam is an animal's mother, MOTHER; M is removed from its front

annotation.surface: A different dam built without any stonework.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Dam' and 'masonry' paint a wall across a river; a dam is also a female parent of livestock, a mother.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: 'the other route' is the alternative route.

entries.clue: Lottery? Getting only first of numbers sucked! (5)

annotation.surface: A lottery player matching only the first number and grumbling that it sucked.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sucked' reads as slang for was rubbish; it is the physical sense, as air is drawn into the lungs.
annotation.definitionFit: Air drawn in through a straw is sucked in.

entries.clue: A fancy uniform (5)

annotation.surface: A smart uniform.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface pairs 'fancy' and 'uniform' as adjective and noun; 'fancy' is the verb and 'uniform' is the adjective.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: uniform things do not vary, like peas in a pod.

entries.clue: The present is so non-U, one admitted (4)

indicatorNotes.non-U: 'non-U' reads literally as 'no U', so that letter goes
indicatorNotes.admitted: to be admitted is to be let in, so I goes inside

blocks.note: so and thus are synonyms; without U it is THS

annotation.surface: Someone sniffing that a gift is vulgar but accepting it anyway.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Non-U' is old British slang for not upper class; here it simply means without the letter U. 'The present' is this, as in this time.
annotation.definitionFit: 'This' refers to the present one, the one here now.

entries.clue: Bow man has no use for this long tie (5)

blocks.clueFragment: Bow man has no use for this
blocks.note: a Cockney drops his aitches, so has no use for H
to itch for something is to long for it

annotation.surface: An archer who never wears a long tie.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bow man' looks like an archer; Bow is a district of east London, and a Cockney born within the sound of Bow Bells famously drops H.
annotation.definitionFit: To hitch something is to tie it, as a horse is hitched to a post.

entries.clue: Criminal last seen crossing island to get key (9)

indicatorNotes.Criminal: the letters are crooked, so disordered
indicatorNotes.crossing: the letters go across the island, taking I inside

blocks.note: standard abbreviation, added to the fodder

annotation.surface: A fugitive last spotted crossing to an island to pick up a key.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Criminal' and 'last seen' read as a wanted notice; 'key' is the adjective, meaning vital.
annotation.definitionFit: Key and essential both mean crucial.

entries.clue: Breath-taking southern Republican involved in revolt (10)

indicatorNotes.involved in: the R goes inside the revolt

blocks.note: an uprising is a revolt; R goes inside it

annotation.surface: A Southern politician joining an uprising.
annotation.walkthrough: The hyphen in 'Breath-taking' is fair: something surprising takes your breath away.
annotation.definitionFit: Breathtaking and surprising both describe something astonishing.

entries.clue: Bank of river by cathedral city (4)

blocks.note: the Cambridgeshire city with a famous cathedral

annotation.surface: A riverbank beside a cathedral town.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bank of river' reads as a riverbank; 'Bank' is the verb, as in bank on someone. ELY is a small English cathedral city near Cambridge.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: to bank on something is to depend on it.
